title: An eagle for Xi, pandas for America and a changing world order
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
An eagle for Xi, pandas for America and a changing world order

Trump gave Xi a bald eagle. Xi promised America two pandas. Behind the diplomatic symbolism sits a larger shift: China’s international standing is improving as trust in the United States declines.

Actual Article Body:
September 30, 2026

Trump gave Xi a bald eagle. Xi promised America two pandas. Behind the diplomatic symbolism sits a larger shift: China’s international standing is improving as trust in the United States declines.

President Donald Trump presented a statue of a bald eagle to President Xi Jinping when they met in Washington on 24 September saying that he hoped it would find a “nice place” in Beijing. The gift of an eagle, the national symbol of the USA, was clearly full of meaning, but different people may have different interpretations of the exchange. (By the way, bald eagles are not bald. They have white ‘bald’ heads.)

This was the second meeting this year between the two superpower heads, coming at a critical juncture when the world faces a looming energy crunch, a debt crisis, continuing wars in the Ukraine, Palestine and Iran, and global concern about AI regulation. It was a strangely muted occasion, largely due to the American press boycott of the White House.

The gift of a bald eagle statue to the visiting Chinese leader is not a Trojan horse, signifying expansionist intent, but surely indicates that Trump hopes that Xi will respect Washington’s views on international affairs. This is not likely to happen. I suspect that Xi, when he unpacks the eagle statue back home in Beijing, will think, “Who is to blame for the present global chaos? Surely, he should take the lead in resolving it.”

Who could blame him for thinking this? China did not invade Iran. China continues to support the United Nations and the international rules-based order. Xi told Trump and the world, “China has . . . consistently played a constructive role in easing tensions and de-escalating the situation.” The consistent Chinese position is that they are a dependable and reliable nation. While building defence capabilities, Beijing has held them in reserve, while the US, with a more powerful military force, deployed everything but still proved incapable of winning against Iran (ranked 16th in the world by the Global Firepower Index) or of opening the Strait of Hormuz to facilitate the global oil trade.

At the same time as waging war on Iran, Trump also picked a fight with Canada, threatened to invade Greenland, scaled back joint military exercises with South Korea, and exacerbated tensions with others through irrational tariff policies. All the countries affected by these decisions were in the past allies of the United States, but their support is no longer unconditional, if it ever was. Meantime, Xi has been travelling across Asia and strengthening ties through groupings such as BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), raising its international standing.

Of course, the situation in Ukraine must be blamed on Russian President Vladimir Putin rather than on Trump, but Trump provided intelligence to Ukraine, allowed American weapons to be purchased for them, cut direct economic and military assistance, and opposed Ukraine joining NATO. China, by contrast, claims neutrality in this conflict and advocates for peace talks.

In Sudan, in Yemen, and across Africa and Latin America, economies are collapsing and social tensions are rife. Trump destroyed potential instruments of influence such as the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), which might have offered practical assistance. He abolished US government-funded broadcast organisations like Voice of America, Radio Free Asia, and Radio Free Europe, greatly diminishing American soft power. While China deployed initiatives like the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), institutions like the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), and media outlets like the state-run international broadcaster CGTN, and Chinese bilateral international aid in 2024 reached US$3.5 billion, an increase of 16 per cent over the previous year, Trump fired scores of diplomats.
